A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, algorithms, and Appendices A–C support reliable comparison, including matching material relocated in v3.

before.justification: v2 reports original Othello analyses of legal-move generation, structural confidence, attention-head pruning, and training/test sequence distributions.

after.justification: v3 retains original Othello results and adds original Chess evaluations and a recovered causal-graph example using a previously trained model.

M1.justification: The attention-derived covariance, per-head recursive ICD procedure, and confidence score R = Hind − Hdep remain unchanged, including the appendix algorithms. The expanded explanation and omitted explicit entropy sums do not establish a changed computational procedure.

E1.justification: v3 adds Chess as an evaluated domain alongside Othello, using a GPT trained on approximately 2.9 million real games and synthetic legal-move sequences. This substantially broadens the game rules and input environments tested. The real-game training versus random-legal-move testing distinction already existed in v2.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparison methods remain the different CI-conditioning restrictions and low- versus high-confidence head pruning. The newly examined Chess GPT is another subject of analysis, rather than a competing causal-discovery method. No comparator is added to the retained ablations.

E3.justification: The added Chess evaluation introduces a 10–40-move window and, in Appendix B.1, 10,000 samples for lengths up to 15 instead of the generally stated 1,000. The retained Othello protocol still uses 1,000 sequence prefixes and a CI threshold of 0.01; their relocation does not establish a protocol revision.

E4.justification: v3 adds a Chess case study connecting recovered graph edges to particular moves in Figure 6. It removes the length-10 Othello head-pruning panel from v2 Figure 5. The CI-conditioning ablation and the remaining head-pruning analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report 95% confidence intervals from an unpaired t-test for the CI-conditioning analysis. Neither adds repeated-run counts, seeds, or another uncertainty-estimation practice. The larger Chess test sample is an evaluation-design addition, not a repeated-run count.

E6.justification: v3 adds six Chess confidence-versus-accuracy curves, a legal-move accuracy curve showing degradation with sequence length, and a recovered Chess graph. Retained Othello plots and reported values, including 95% overall accuracy and 88% at length 15, are unchanged. The length-10 Othello confidence and pruning panels are omitted; the former showed no clear confidence–accuracy trend in v2.

T1.justification: v3 adds Equation 9, explicitly relating normalized attention to the inverse SCM matrix after removing rows and columns corresponding to hidden nodes. This extends the stated mathematical correspondence. The linear-Gaussian assumptions, Markov and faithfulness definitions, and existing derivations remain; no new proof is supplied.

C1.justification: v2's abstract restricts zero-shot structure learning to in-distribution sequences; v3 refers generally to input sequences and explicitly frames the confidence–legality claim around out-of-distribution inputs. The central causal-world-model contribution remains, with its empirical scope now including Chess.

C2.justification: v3 removes the specific short-Othello qualification and associated surface-statistics explanation from the confidence analysis, although general opening-move memorization discussion survives in Appendix B.1. It adds Chess-specific applicability reasoning for excluding very short sequences and limiting longer sequences because games can terminate.

D1.justification: v3 explicitly documents uniform sampling among legal moves and provides the Chess model source, training-corpus size, and short-sequence sample-count exception. Conversely, the explicit sums defining Hind and Hdep after v2 Equation 9 disappear, leaving the retained confidence score less fully specified. Neither version supplies code-access or hardware details.

R1.justification: The cited works and positioning relative to ABCD and earlier world-representation studies remain the same. Toshniwal et al.'s Chess work was already cited in v2. Creating a separate Related Work section and changing citation formatting do not introduce new research positioning.

P1.justification: v3 substantially reorganizes the narrative: it separates Related Work, expands the GPT–SCM explanation, places ablations before the main confidence evaluation, moves substantial setup discussion into Appendix B.1, and places references before the appendices. The title, abstract, and conclusion are also revised.

P2.justification: v3 adds the GPT–SCM schematic and Chess example, combines retained Othello and new Chess results in Figures 5 and 7, and compresses the remaining pruning panels into one row. Existing plots are relocated or rearranged, while the proceedings layout introduces running headers and single-column appendices.

improvement.justification: The Chess results broaden empirical support beyond one game, and Figure 2 makes the GPT–SCM correspondence easier to follow. However, v3 removes the documented length-10 Othello exception and its qualification while making the abstract less restrictive, and it omits explicit entropy calculations. These changes create material tradeoffs between broader validation and reduced transparency and reproducibility; a reliable net quality direction is unclear.
